sections.heading: Model types and examples
paragraphs: Fishwick’s categories include declarative models focused on states and events; functional models connect components directionally through mathematical relationships; constraint models emphasize relationships and physical balances rather than direction; spatial models represent spaces or entities within spaces. Page 5 repeats the functional definition under declarative models; use the state-event description and page 6 examples instead.

The Easy Pass deceleration functional diagram uses a = dv/dt and v = dx/dt: an acceleration signal is integrated to velocity (initial condition v₀), then velocity to position. The constraint example adds ½mv² = F_f d; for constant friction magnitude and stopping from initial speed v, d = mv²/(2F_f). For example, m = 1000 kg, v = 10 m/s, F_f = 5000 N gives d = 10 m. This assumes friction accounts for the kinetic energy lost.

sections.heading: Conceptual and hybrid models
paragraphs: A conceptual model communicates the target system’s main functionality and distinctive qualities quickly, often informally in a picture or one or two paragraphs. The Easy Pass example uses both textual and graphical representations.

A multimodel or hybrid connects several models, potentially of different types, in a network. Different abstractions support different questions or different phases of a complex system. In a concept map, nodes represent concepts or elements, directed arrows indicate interactions, and arrow labels describe their nature.

sections.heading: Formal and semiformal tools
paragraphs: A formalism specifies precise rules for modeling and simulation; its formal models support unambiguous mathematical analysis, often automated, but can be complex and tedious to design and implement. Semiformal representations trade some precision for ease of use while retaining some analytical capability. The slide’s phrase ‘less unambiguity’ is confusing; the intended contrast is less precision than formal models.

UML is a standardized, semiformal, object-oriented graphic notation for system and software structure and behavior. The slide lists use cases, activity diagrams, class diagrams, sequence diagrams, and statecharts.

sections.heading: Verification and validation
paragraphs: Verification checks whether conceptual-model requirements were correctly translated into the executable model and whether it runs reliably. Techniques include automated debugging, peer code review, and stress tests at minimum and maximum boundary conditions; debugging may struggle with semantic errors.

Validation asks whether the model approximates its target system sufficiently well to provide useful results. Compare model and target outputs statistically when possible; when the target does not exist, use a similar system or expert judgment. Expert judgment of outputs is face validation.

sections.heading: Operations research
paragraphs: Operations research applies mathematical models to complex systems to optimize performance and support decisions, such as maximizing profit or minimizing cost. Formulate the problem, develop a mathematical model, then solve it to search for an optimum.
Linear programming is a deterministic method using a linear objective and linear constraints. Stochastic operations-research methods include Markov chains and queuing theory.

sections.heading: Simulink and worked block examples
paragraphs: Simulink integrates with MATLAB and provides a graphical editor, customizable block libraries, and solvers for modeling and simulating dynamic systems. MATLAB algorithms can be included in models and results exported to MATLAB. Applications include pre-hardware exploration, reusable components, hardware-in-the-loop testing, and large simulations on multicore desktops, clusters, or the cloud.

In the arithmetic block example, (1+100)+(50+100)−75−10 = 166 and 166×(10×1) = 1660. A greater-than comparison with 5000 returns 0 (false). In the other example, √16 + 3² + sign(−5) = 4+9−1 = 12, so equality to 12 returns 1 (true).
